subject: Quantitative Aptitude
topic: Profit and Loss II — marked price, discount, successive discount, dishonest dealer
description: Profit & Loss advanced: marked price, discount %, successive discounts, false weight, profit on cost vs selling price, goods damaged in transit.

questions.stem: A shopkeeper marks an article 40% above cost price and offers a 20% discount. What is the profit percentage?

options.option_text: 12% profit
20% profit — this ignores the discount effect on SP
8% profit — incorrect calculation of successive effects
No profit/loss — wrong; MP and discount are not equal offsets

questions.explanation: SETUP: Let CP = 100. MP = 140 (40% above CP). After 20% discount: SP = 140 × 0.8 = 112. Profit = 112 − 100 = 12. Profit% = 12%. FORMULA SHORTCUT: Profit% = (1 + m/100)(1 − d/100) − 1 = 1.4 × 0.8 − 1 = 1.12 − 1 = 0.12 = 12%. TRAP: students add/subtract markup and discount directly (40 − 20 = 20% profit) — WRONG because they operate on different bases.

questions.stem: Two successive discounts of 30% and 20% are equivalent to a single discount of:

options.option_text: 44% single equivalent discount
50% — this is simply adding 30+20, which overcounts
42% — underestimates the compounding of successive discounts
46% — overestimates the interaction between the two discounts

questions.explanation: FORMULA: Single equivalent discount = x + y − xy/100 = 30 + 20 − (30×20)/100 = 50 − 6 = 44%. VERIFICATION: MP = 100. After 30%: 70. After 20% on 70: 70 × 0.8 = 56. Single discount = 100 − 56 = 44%. RULE: successive discounts CANNOT be simply added because the second discount applies to a reduced price. PYQ ANGLE: 3-discount chains also possible; apply formula twice.

questions.stem: A dishonest dealer uses a 900 g weight while claiming to sell 1 kg. If he buys at ₹40/kg and sells at ₹40/kg (no markup), what is his actual profit percentage?

options.option_text: 11.11% profit — he gives less than claimed while receiving full payment
10% profit — underestimates since 100g short out of 900g (not 1000g) basis
No profit — same buy/sell price seems like break-even but ignores cheating
9% profit — wrong denominator used in the profit fraction

questions.explanation: CHEATING PROFIT: He claims to sell 1000 g but actually gives 900 g. He collects ₹40 per 'kg'. COST: 900 g at ₹40/kg = ₹36. REVENUE: ₹40 (customer pays for 1000 g). PROFIT = 40 − 36 = ₹4. PROFIT% on cost = 4/36 × 100 = 11.11%. FORMULA: Profit% = (error / true weight − error) × 100 = (100/900) × 100 = 11.11%. ALTERNATIVE FORM: (claimed − actual) / actual × 100. PYQ: dishonest dealer problems are standard in IBPS PO/CGL quant; always compute profit on COST not on claimed weight.

questions.stem: A trader sells goods at a 25% profit on cost. What is the profit expressed as a percentage of the selling price?

options.option_text: 20% of selling price
25% of selling price — same ratio applies only when CP=SP, which contradicts a profit
33.33% of selling price — this is the ratio when profit = 1/3 of CP, not 1/4
16.67% of selling price — this corresponds to a ~20% profit on CP, not 25%

questions.explanation: CP = 100, SP = 125 (25% profit on CP). Profit as % of SP = (25/125) × 100 = 20%. CONVERSION FORMULA: If profit% on CP = x, then profit% on SP = x/(100+x) × 100. Here: 25/125 × 100 = 20%. REVERSE: profit% on SP = y → profit% on CP = y/(100−y) × 100. PYQ ANGLE: examiners frequently swap the base (CP vs SP); always check which base the question asks about.

questions.stem: A dealer buys 100 oranges for ₹120 and sells 80 oranges for ₹120 (the rest spoil). What is the overall profit or loss percentage?

options.option_text: No profit/no loss — cost and revenue are both ₹120
25% loss — mistakenly treats 20 spoilt as a cash loss
20% loss — incorrect calculation ignoring matching cost and revenue
25% profit — reverses the comparison direction entirely

questions.explanation: COST = ₹120 (for 100 oranges). REVENUE = ₹120 (selling 80 oranges). PROFIT/LOSS = 120 − 120 = 0. RESULT: exactly break-even (0% profit/loss). INSIGHT: The fact that 20 units spoilt is already accounted for in the lower revenue. The CP per sold unit is higher (₹120/80 = ₹1.50 vs ₹120/100 = ₹1.20 buy price) but total cash in = total cash out. TRAP: students try to compute per-unit profit when the question is about total cash flow.

questions.stem: An article is sold at a 10% loss. Had it been sold for ₹90 more, there would have been a 20% profit. What is the cost price?

options.option_text: ₹300 — derived from the ₹90 gap spanning 30% of CP
₹450 — arithmetic error in computing the percentage gap
₹270 — confuses absolute difference with the loss amount only
₹360 — wrong base percentage used for the difference calculation

questions.explanation: Let CP = x. SP at 10% loss = 0.9x. SP at 20% profit = 1.2x. Difference = 1.2x − 0.9x = 0.3x = ₹90. → x = 90/0.3 = ₹300. VERIFICATION: CP=300; Loss SP=270; Profit SP=360; 360−270=90 ✓. EXAM PATTERN: 'had it been sold for ₹Y more/less' questions always set up a linear equation on the CP — the difference in SPs equals the difference in profit/loss percentages × CP.

questions.stem: A shopkeeper sells two articles each at ₹1,200. On one he gains 20% and on the other he loses 20%. What is the net result of the two transactions?

options.option_text: Net loss of 4% — identical SP with equal % gain/loss always results in a loss equal to (x²/100)%
No profit/no loss — the gains and losses appear symmetric but they are not
Net gain of 4% — reverses the direction of the classic equal-% result (not this)
Net loss of 2% — underestimates the compounding of different CP bases (not this)

questions.explanation: CLASSIC TRAP: When SAME SP, equal % gain and loss ALWAYS gives a net LOSS. FORMULA: Loss% = (x²/100)% where x = 20. Loss% = 400/100 = 4%. VERIFICATION: Gain article: SP=1200, profit=20% → CP₁=1200/1.2=1000. Loss article: SP=1200, loss=20% → CP₂=1200/0.8=1500. Total CP=2500, Total SP=2400. Loss=100. Loss%=100/2500×100=4% ✓. PYQ: this is one of the most frequently tested P&L traps across IBPS, SSC, and CAT; the asymmetry arises because the CPs are different even though SPs are equal.
